title: Two-wheel hand cart
summary: Build a two-wheel pull cart from salvaged wheels, steel tube or timber, and bolts. One person can move 100–200 kg on a decent track with far less effort than carrying. Balance the load over the axle and support bicycle hub axles on both sides.

materials.item: Wheels, matched pair: 20–29 inch bike wheels, wheelbarrow, mower, or mobility-scooter wheels (pneumatic is best)
Axle: solid steel rod or long bolt, 16 mm for 100 kg, 20 mm for 200 kg (unless using bike hubs)
Steel or aluminium tube or angle 25–40 mm for the frame and handle (or 50 × 50 mm timber)
Deck: plywood 12–18 mm or steel mesh
Steel plate for bike-hub dropouts or axle brackets, 3–5 mm
Bolts M8–M10 with washers and lock nuts

steps.text: Decide the load, width and handle. Keep it no wider than about 80 cm for trails and doorways. Plan for 100–150 kg on bike wheels, 200+ kg on wheelbarrow, mower or scooter wheels.
Check the wheels: they should spin freely without wobble or grinding, tyres hold air, spokes all tight. Grease or replace bearings that grind.

Bike wheels: keep the hub axles and make a slotted dropout plate for each side of each hub, so every hub is held at both ends like in a bike frame. Other wheels: use one through-axle with washers and locking nuts or pins.
steps.warn: A bike hub axle held on one side only bends and fails under load.

steps.text: Cut the frame: a rectangle with cross members every 30–40 cm. File every cut edge smooth.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection and gloves when grinding or cutting: sparks and razor-sharp burrs.

steps.text: Place the axle or dropouts slightly behind the middle of the deck, so that when loaded about 5–10% of the weight rests on the handle.
Bolt the joints with washers and lock nuts. Add a diagonal brace or a triangular plate at each corner so the frame can't fold into a parallelogram.
Fit the deck. Add sides 20–40 cm high if you'll carry loose items.
Fit the handle at the front: a single pull bar 1–1.2 m long, or a T-bar so two people can pull. Pad the grip.
Add a stand or two short legs at the front so the cart sits level when parked.
Fit tie-down points at each corner.
Test with half the planned load over 100 m of rough ground. Check bolts, wheels and frame for bending, then try the full load.
steps.warn: A loaded cart running downhill can knock you over and run you down. On slopes keep the cart below you and hold it back, or drag a brake.

steps.text: Load heavy items low and over the axle, light items at the ends. Check tyre pressure and bolts before each long trip.

notes:
## Balance
Handle force ≈ load × (distance from axle to load's centre) ÷ (distance from axle to the handle grip). With 150 kg centred 10 cm ahead of the axle and the grip 1.5 m from the axle: 150 × 0.1 ÷ 1.5 = 10 kg on the handle. Load too far back and the handle flips up; too far forward and you carry the load yourself.

## Wheels
| Wheel | Load per wheel | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 26–29 inch mountain or hybrid bike | about 50–80 kg | Rolls easily over rough ground; weak sideways, so take turns gently |
| 20 inch bike | about 50–70 kg | Stronger, lower |
| Wheelbarrow (pneumatic, 14–16 inch) | 100–150 kg | Tough; slower rolling |
| Mobility scooter or mower | 75–150 kg | Small; good on hard surfaces |

Big wheels roll over rocks and ruts; small wheels get stuck.

## Axle size
With a wheel 5 cm out from its support, the load on each wheel bends the axle. Mild steel rod: 16 mm carries about 50 kg per wheel comfortably, 20 mm about 100 kg per wheel, with a safety margin for bumps. Keep wheels close to the frame. Don't let threads sit inside a wheel bearing.

## Variations
- **Bike trailer:** the same cart with a hitch arm to the bike's seat post or rear axle. Keep within the trailer's rating and the bike's: Burley rates its Flatbed cargo trailer at 45 kg (100 lb), at up to 24 km/h on smooth straight roads and 8 km/h on turns or rough ground, with 1–9 kg pressing on the hitch when loaded (Burley Flatbed). A home-built trailer has no rating: start light, test it, and brake early.
- **Shopping cart:** swap its small casters for bigger pneumatic wheels and it handles rough ground.
- **Travois or sled:** two poles or a sheet dragged on the ground, when there are no wheels.

## Punctures
No patches? Stuff the tyre tightly with rope, rags or foam to make a solid tyre. It rides harder but won't go flat.

## If you lack a part
- No tube: timber frame with bolts through, and steel angle for the axle brackets.
- No bolts: lash joints tightly with wire or rope, and re-tighten often.

sources.title: Burley Flatbed: Burley Design, Flatbed Owner's Instruction and Safety Manual (2023)
